Approval of Annual Report

The Board of Directors (‘the Board’) is pleased to present the annual report, including the
financial statements of Partners Life Limited (‘the Company’) for the year ended 31 March
2025.

The Company is a climate reporting entity for the purposes of the Financial Markets
Conduct Act 2013 and has elected to include a copy of the Climate Statement for the year
ended 31 March 2025 within this annual report.

The shareholder of the Company has agreed to apply the reporting concessions available
under s211(3) of the Companies Act 1993. Accordingly, there is no additional statutory
information required to be included in the Annual Report other than the financial
statements for the year ended 31 March 2025, the Independent Auditor's Report on those

Notes to the 
Financial Statements
1. Reporting entity
The Company is a profit-oriented company domiciled in New Zealand and registered under the Companies Act 
1993.   
Financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2025 (‘the financial statements’) are presented for the 
Company. The Company is 100% owned by Partners Group Holdings Limited (‘PGHL’), with its ultimate holding 
company being Dai-ichi Life International Holdings LLC (‘DIL’).
The Company is a reporting entity for the purposes of the Companies Act 1993 and the Financial Markets 
Conduct Act 2013, and its financial statements comply with these Acts.  
The Company is a licenced life insurer under the Insurance (Prudential Supervision) Act 2010 (‘IPSA’) and these 
Financial Statements also comply with that act. 
The annual report was authorised for issue by the Board on 13 June 2025.
2. Statement of compliance and reporting framework
The financial statements have been prepared in accordance with New Zealand Generally Accepted Accounting 
Practice (‘NZ GAAP’), as a for-profit entity, and comply with International Financial Reporting Standards (‘IFRS’) 
and the New Zealand Equivalents to International Financial Reporting Standards (‘NZ IFRS’). 
With the agreement of the sole shareholder, the Company has taken advantage of the reporting concessions 
available to it under section 211(3) of the Companies Act 1993.
3. Basis of preparation
The financial statements have been prepared on a going concern basis. 
The financial statements have been prepared on a historical cost basis except for: 
—
insurance and reinsurance contract assets and liabilities which are stated at actuarially assessed values 
in accordance with New Zealand Equivalent to International Financial Reporting Standard 17 Insurance 
Contracts (‘NZ IFRS 17’);
—
investments in government bonds which are designated, at inception, as at fair value through profit or 
loss; and
—
lease liabilities which are measured at the present value of the lease payments.  
The financial statements are presented in New Zealand dollars (‘NZD’), which is the Company’s functional 
currency. 
Accounting Standards or Interpretations adopted in the current year
The accounting policies adopted are consistent with those applied in the prior year, except as described below. 
Changes in accounting standards
Disclosure of fees for audit firms’ services – Amendments to FRS-44 New Zealand Additional Disclosures 
(FRS-44)
Amendments to FRS-44 were issued in May 2023 that require an entity to describe the services provided by its 
auditor or review firm and to disclose the fees incurred for those services using prescribed categories. The 
Company adopted the Amendments to FRS-44 from 1 April 2024. Refer to note 8 for further details.
Amendments to NZ IAS 12 – International Tax Reform Pillar 2 Model Rules
The Company adopted the International Tax Reform Pillar 2 Model Rules (amendments to NZ IAS 12) effective 
from 1 April 2024. The amendments provide a temporary and mandatory exemption from deferred tax accounting 
with respect to Pillar 2 income taxes and require new disclosures in the financial statements in relation to the 
implementation of Pillar 2 Model Rules published by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and 
Development (‘OECD’). The Company has applied the exemption. Further information on the Company’s position 
as at 31 March 2025 is provided in note 9.
10

3. Basis of preparation (continued)
There have been no other changes to accounting policies or new or amended standards issued that had a 
material impact on these financial statements. 
There are a number of standards, amendments, and interpretations which have been approved but are not yet 
effective. The Company expects to adopt these when they become due for adoption and is assessing their 
impact on the financial statements. 
Where applicable comparative information has been reclassified to ensure alignment with presentation and 
disclosure in the current reporting period. These reclassifications have no impact on net profit/(loss) after taxation 
or net assets.
4. Critical accounting judgements and key sources of estimation uncertainty
The preparation of financial statements requires management to make judgements, estimates, and assumptions 
that affect the application of accounting policies and the reported amounts of assets, liabilities, income, and 
expenses. Actual results may differ from these estimates.  
Insurance contract assets and liabilities  
Judgements made in applying NZ IFRS 17 are described in note 10.
The key areas where judgements are made in respect of insurance contract assets and liabilities are:    
—
classification of insurance and reinsurance contracts and whether the contracts transfer significant 
insurance risk as well as whether there are contracts that contain direct participation features;
—
the level of aggregation of insurance and reinsurance contracts, including identifying portfolios or groups  
of contracts that are onerous on initial recognition and those that have no possibility of subsequently 
becoming onerous;
—
measurement of insurance and reinsurance contracts, including determining the discount rates, the 
techniques for estimating risk adjustments for non-financial risk and the coverage units provided under a 
contract.
Insurance contract assets and liabilities are valued using actuarial methods that take into account the risks and 
uncertainties of the particular classes of insurance business written. Refer to note 10. 
The key factors that affect the estimated value of the insurance contract assets and liabilities are:  
—
the cost of providing benefits and administering the insurance contracts; 
—
the costs incurred in acquiring the insurance policies (acquisition costs), including adviser commissions, 
underwriting and policy issue costs;  
—
mortality and morbidity experience on life insurance products;  
—
discontinuance experience which affects the ability to recover acquisition costs;
—
recoverability of the asset for insurance acquisition cash flows;
—
the timing and duration of claims and resulting cash flows which affects the determination of the liability 
for incurred claims and the liability for remaining coverage;
—
rate of renewal of insurance contracts;
—
future expenses and operating environment;
—
contract boundaries for insurance and reinsurance contracts;
—
reinsurance arrangements and timing of future cash flows under these arrangements, which include 
reinsurance expense, reinsurance recoveries, and reinsurance commission revenue;
—
future premium rates;
—
a risk adjustment reflecting the uncertainty of the amount and timing of cash flows arising from non-
financial risks related to insurance contracts;  and
—
other factors such as regulation, competition, inflation, interest rates, and general economic conditions 
which are used in the valuation of insurance contract assets and liabilities.  
Notes to the Financial Statements (continued)

5. Risk management 
The Company’s risk management strategy is designed to implement a consistent and effective approach to 
identify, evaluate, and respond to key risks that may impact business objectives. This enterprise risk 
management framework is built on a three lines of defence risk management model and is supported by the key 
components, including:
Risk Appetite 
The implementation of the business strategy is kept within the Company’s Risk Appetite Statements (‘RAS’) to 
ensure the delivery of best-in-market life and health insurance to customers and sustainable growth in 
shareholder value while managing enterprise risks. The Company’s appetite is set and regularly reviewed by the 
Board and monitored through the Risk Committee.  
Risk Governance 
The Company’s Risk Committee is chartered to monitor and assess the Company’s compliance with significant 
laws and regulations, identify key risks, and initiate and monitor actions to mitigate these risks in line with the 
Company’s Risk Management Programme. The Risk Management Programme is also regularly reviewed to 
ensure it continues to be relevant in effectively managing our risks. The Risk Committee is chaired by an 
independent, non-executive director.  
Management-level committees are in place to deliberate on key risk matters, the primary one being the 
Management Risk Committee (‘MRC’) that meets at least four times per year and supports the Risk Committee in 
the execution of its duties. An Asset and Liability Management Committee (‘ALCO’) also meets on a regular basis 
to monitor and manage financial risks. The ALCO reports to the Board on a regular basis. A Statement of 
Investment Policy and Objectives (‘SIPO’), a Capital Management Policy (‘CMP’), and a Treasury Policy establish 
parameters for the management of investment assets and solvency capital.  The SIPO and CMP are both 
approved by the Board. The Product and Pricing Committee is responsible for oversight of the insurance RAS 
measures and the Executive Committee is responsible for oversight of the strategic RAS measures. 
Risk Culture 
Risk culture is formed by values and behaviours that shape decisions around day-to-day risk-taking activities. 
The Company maintains a strong risk culture that is underpinned by overall Company values and is supported by 
effective communication and training, and tone from the top.  
Risk Management Process 
A comprehensive and consistent process is applied in the identification, assessment, management, and 
monitoring of risks across the Company. Its implementation employs the use of an integrated governance, risk 
management, and compliance system, which also houses the Enterprise Risk Register and Sub-Risks Register. 
Collectively, these form part of the Company’s overall risk and control environment which are regularly reviewed 
and discussed in the MRC and Risk Committee meetings.  
The financial condition and operating results of the Company are exposed to a number of risks, the primary risks 
being insurance, market, credit, liquidity, and capital risk. 
Insurance risk  
Insurance risk is risk, other than financial risk, that is transferred from the holder of a contract to the issuer.   
The Company’s objectives in managing insurance risk are:  
—
to continuously meet internal and external solvency requirements; 
—
to utilise reinsurance to keep the retained portion of claims in line with the Company’s risk appetite;  
—
to set premium rates, based on expected claims and expenses, that will ensure an appropriate return on 
capital; and  
—
to maintain a sound internal control environment.   
The Company takes a sustainable approach to all aspects of its product portfolio, including new business 
underwriting, and the management of its in-force book, regularly reviewing assumptions against experience. 
Assumptions are based on the Company’s own experience, industry benchmarks, and reinsurer data to reflect 
the Company’s risk profile as well as observable market trends.  
Notes to the Financial Statements (continued)

A number of variables give rise to insurance risk:   
—
The risks associated with mortality and morbidity: Higher mortality rates and/or an increased incidence

—
Policy lapses and cancellations: The impact of lapses and rate of policy cancellations depends upon the 
type of contract and duration in force, but generally an increase in lapses and cancellations will reduce 
profit and shareholder’s equity.  
—
Expense levels: If expenses are higher than assumed levels this will reduce profit and shareholder’s

Insurance risk management  
a)
Reinsurance 
Individual and group risk 
The Company has entered into reinsurance treaties for the majority of individual risk sold. The treaties are 
designed to limit the Company’s exposure to insurance risk to a level appropriate to its age and capital base. 
The individual risk treaties meet the definition of an insurance contract under NZ IFRS 17 as there is a significant 
transfer of insurance risk from the Company to the reinsurers through the reinsurance of an agreed percentage of 
insurance risks on all reinsured benefits. Further, the reinsurers bear lapse risk through the treaties. If a reinsurer 
ceases to take new business under the treaties, it remains on risk for policies previously reinsured.
Reinsurance premiums are paid to the reinsurers for benefits reinsured. A defined percentage of claims paid on 
reinsured benefits is recoverable from the reinsurers. The reinsurers pay the Company a commission on the 
issue of new business covered by the treaties which contributes towards the costs of acquiring new insurance 
business. 
The Company has entered into separate reinsurance treaties for group risk; the treaties are designed to limit the 
Company’s exposure to insurance risk arising from group business. 
Notes to the Financial Statements (continued)
13

5. Risk management  (continued)
Concentrations of risk   
Concentrations of insurance risk arise from:
—
Customers with large sums assured: this risk is mitigated through surplus reinsurance, which limits the 
Company’s exposure for lump sum claims to a maximum retention per benefit per life assured.
—
Customers concentrated in a country or region that could be affected by pandemic: the Company has 
entered into a reinsurance treaty which mitigates the risk of significant losses due to a pandemic event.
—
Customers concentrated in a geographical area: the Company has entered into a reinsurance treaty 
which mitigates the risk of significant losses due to a catastrophic accidental event.
b)
Underwriting processes  
Underwriting decisions are made in accordance with rules and procedures detailed in the Company’s 
underwriting manual.  
Such rules and procedures include limits to delegated authorities and signing powers for individual underwriters 
and limits over which individual cases must be referred to the Company’s reinsurers for an underwriting 
decision.  
Underwriting is monitored by the Underwriting Leadership Team to ensure adequate controls are in place over 
the various processes and the effectiveness of those controls. The Company’s reinsurers and underwriting 
management team carry out regular audits to ensure underwriting decisions made are in accordance with rules, 
limits, and the Company’s underwriting philosophy.  
c)
Claims management  
Claims management procedures are in place to ensure the timely and accurate payment of all valid claims in 
accordance with policy conditions.  
The Company is committed to the fair treatment of customers. The Company’s Fair Conduct Programme (‘FCP’) 
describes expectations for staff and intermediaries to meet the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 (‘FMCA’) fair 
conduct principle and the key policies, processes, systems, and controls that are in place to support fair 
treatment of customers. A Customer Outcomes Review Committee, comprising some of the key management 
personnel (‘KMP’), is responsible for providing a forum to discuss and make decisions relating to re-underwriting, 
complex claims and customer-related issues. These could be, but are not limited to:   
—
referred claims;    
—
claims where there is possible non-disclosure, misrepresentation, or possibly fraud;
—
significant or serious customer complaints that are unable to be resolved and a letter of deadlock needs 
to be issued so the customer can escalate to the external disputes resolution scheme;
—
issues related to the treatment of vulnerable customers; and
—
significant complaints against third party advisers.

Interest rate risk management 
New Zealand government bonds are used to minimise interest rate exposures resulting from movements in 
incurred claim reserves, net of reinsurance. To the extent that maturity profiles are aligned, interest rate 
movement impacts on incurred claims and reinsurance recoverable on those incurred claims will be materially 
offset by opposite impacts on New Zealand government bond yields and therefore values. As interest rates and 
net claim reserves change, the government bond portfolio is rebalanced through sales and purchases to ensure 
the net interest rate exposure of net claim reserves and government bonds remains minimised.

Credit risk  
Credit risk is the risk of loss arising from the failure of a counterparty to meet their contractual obligations as they 
relate to amounts recognised at balance date. The Company is exposed to credit risk from the investment of 
surplus capital, reinsurance recoverable, and receivables (amounts due from advisers).  
The maximum exposure to credit risk at balance date for each class of financial asset is the carrying amount of 
those assets as indicated in the table below.  
Credit risk management  
The Company manages credit risk by adopting a conservative investment philosophy and spreading its 
exposures. The SIPO establishes minimum credit ratings and exposure limits for investment counterparties.  
Surplus capital is invested in call and term deposit facilities, spread across a number of high credit quality New 
Zealand registered banks, as well as New Zealand government bonds of various maturities. Refer to note 12.  
Reinsurance credit risk is managed by considering the current and a potential reinsurer’s credit quality, as 
evidenced by their credit rating and balance sheet strength as well as their reputation in the market for paying 
claims.  
Commission recoveries due from advisers are regularly reviewed and an allowance for expected credit losses is 
raised. Amounts due from advisers are disclosed net of expected credit losses in trade and other receivables.

Liquidity risk  
Liquidity risk is the risk that an entity will encounter difficulty in meeting obligations associated with its financial

investment. New Zealand government bond investment maturities are matched to expected incurred claim 
reserve profiles and are tradable on an active secondary market should additional cash flow be required.   
Term bank deposits are structured so that investments are maturing at regular intervals to accommodate future 
obligations and mitigate cash flow volatility; for example, higher than expected claims.  
The Company monitors liquidity risk by forecasting future daily cash requirements and ALCO regularly reviews

8. Commission and operating expenses
Commission paid to independent advisers, and the Company’s operating expenses, are apportioned between 
directly attributable expenses (‘DAE’) and non-DAE. DAE are then further categorised into acquisition and 
maintenance expenses, which determines the timing of expense recognition. Non-DAE are expensed as

Acquisition expenses 
Acquisition expenses comprise the costs of acquiring new business, including adviser commission and other 
similar advertising, underwriting, sales and distribution costs related to accepting, issuing, and initially recording 
policies, as well as an allocation of overheads. Initial commission is treated as acquisition expenses as it relates 
to activities for selling, underwriting, and commencing groups of insurance contracts and meets the definition of 
insurance acquisition cash flows.
Refer to note 10 for further details on the recognition and allocation of acquisition costs.
Maintenance expenses  
Maintenance expenses comprise the costs of administering policies subsequent to sale, including renewal and as 
earned commission, and all other operating expenses of the Company other than acquisition expenses and those 
categorised as non-DAE. 
Unless directly attributable to specific distribution channels or products, maintenance expenses are allocated to 
portfolios of insurance contracts based on in-force drivers. The specific drivers are determined by the nature of 
the underlying costs, with costs allocated based on rider counts or annual premium income.

10. Insurance and reinsurance contracts
Classification 
The Company issues insurance contracts (e.g. life, disability income, redundancy, total permanent disability, 
trauma, and medical) in the normal course of business, under which it accepts significant insurance risk from its 
policyholders.  
The Company also holds reinsurance contracts with respective reinsurers which constitute a transfer of a portion 
of the underlying insurance risk associated with the products it provides. 
All of the Company’s insurance contracts issued and reinsurance contracts held pass the significant risk transfer 
test and qualified as insurance or reinsurance contracts within the scope of NZ IFRS 17. 
Separation of distinct non-insurance components 
The Company assesses its insurance products to determine whether these contain any distinct non-insurance 
components which must be accounted for under another IFRS rather than NZ IFRS 17. After separating any 
distinct non-insurance components, NZ IFRS 17 requires the Company to apply the standard to the remaining 
components of the insurance contract. Currently, the Company’s insurance products do not include any distinct 
non-insurance components that require separation. 
However, some of the Company’s reinsurance contracts held contain profit commission arrangements. Under 
these arrangements, there is a minimum guaranteed amount that the Company will always receive – either in the 
form of profit commission or another contractual payment, irrespective of the insured event happening. The profit 
commission components have been assessed to be highly interrelated with the insurance components of the 
reinsurance contracts and are, therefore, non-distinct investment components and not accounted for separately. 
Aggregation 
The Company aggregates its insurance contracts issued and its reinsurance contracts held into groups for 
measurement purposes in accordance with the level of aggregation requirements under NZ IFRS 17. The 
Company determines the groups of contracts by first identifying portfolios of contracts subject to similar risks 
which are managed together.  
Insurance contracts 
Each portfolio is divided into groups based on expectations of profitability: 
—
a group of contracts that are onerous at initial recognition (i.e. expected to be loss making); 
—
a group of contracts that, at initial recognition, have no significant possibility of becoming onerous 
subsequently; and 
—
a group of the remaining contracts. 
Reinsurance contracts 
Reinsurance contracts are treated similarly, except that reference to onerous contracts is replaced by reference 
to contracts for which there is a net gain on initial recognition.  
Hence, reinsurance contracts are grouped into the following: 
—
contracts which are in a net gain position on initial recognition; 
—
contracts which have no significant possibility of moving into a net gain position subsequently; and 
—
all remaining contracts. 
Each of the insurance and reinsurance contract groups is then divided into time bound cohorts in which each 
group must not contain contracts issued more than 12 months apart. The Company uses annual cohorts aligned 
with its financial year.

10. Insurance and reinsurance contracts (continued)
Recognition 
Insurance contracts 
The Company recognises groups of insurance contracts that it issues from the earliest of the following: 
—
the beginning of the coverage period of the group of contracts. This is the period during which the 
Company provides services in respect of any premiums within the boundary of the contract. 
—
the date when the first payment from a policyholder in the group of insurance contracts is due; or when 
the first payment is received if there is no due date. 
—
for a group of onerous contracts, as soon as facts and circumstances indicate that the group is onerous. 
Generally, unless an insurance contract is considered onerous, the issue date of the policy is the date of initial 
recognition relative to a policy’s contractual terms. 
Insurance contracts acquired in a transfer of contracts, or a business combination are recognised on the date of 
acquisition. 
Reinsurance contracts 
The Company recognises a group of reinsurance contracts held from the earliest of the following: 
—
the beginning of the coverage period of the group of reinsurance contracts held. However, the Company 
delays the recognition of a group of reinsurance contracts held that provide proportionate coverage until 
the date when any underlying insurance contract is initially recognised, if that date is later than the 
beginning of the coverage period of the group of reinsurance contracts held. 
—
the date the Company recognises an onerous group of underlying insurance contracts if the Company 
entered the related reinsurance contract held in the group of reinsurance contracts held at or before that 
date. 
The Company adds new contracts to the group in the reporting period in which that contract meets one of the 
above recognition criteria. 
Contract boundaries 
The Company includes in the measurement of a group of insurance contracts or reinsurance contracts all the 
future cash flows within the boundary of each contract in the group.  
Insurance contracts 
Cash flows are within the contract boundary for application of NZ IFRS 17 if they arise from substantive rights 
and obligations that exist during the reporting period in which the Company can compel the policyholder to pay 
premiums or it has a substantive obligation to provide services. A substantive obligation to provide services ends 
when: 
—
the Company has the practical ability to reassess the risks of the particular policyholder and can set a 
price or level of benefits that fully reflects those reassessed risks; or 
—
the Company has the practical ability to reassess the risks of the portfolio that contains the contract and 
can set a price or level of benefits that fully reflects the risks of that portfolio, and the pricing of the 
premiums up to the reassessment date does not take into account risks that relate to periods after the 
reassessment date.  
The Company assessed the contract boundary of the Company’s insurance contracts issued as follows: 
—
Yearly Renewable Term (‘YRT’) contracts are generally considered to have a coverage period and 
contract boundary of one year, corresponding to the current policy year. 
—
Level premium contracts and YRT contracts associated with level premium riders, such as accelerated 
benefits, are considered to have a coverage period and contract boundary equivalent to the level 
premium period.

Reinsurance contracts 
Cash flows of reinsurance contracts held are within the contract boundary for application of NZ IFRS 17 if they 
arise from substantive rights and obligations that exist during the reporting period in which the Company is 
compelled to pay reinsurance premiums to the reinsurer, subject only to actions solely within its control, or it has 
a substantive right to receive services from the reinsurer. A substantive right to receive services from the 
reinsurer ends when the reinsurer: 
—
has the practical ability to reassess the risks transferred to it and can set a price or level of benefits that 
fully reflects those reassessed risks; or 
—
has a substantive right to terminate the reinsurance coverage. 
The Company assessed the contract boundaries of reinsurance contracts based on the individual terms of each 
contract. For the most significant reinsurance treaties, the resulting contract boundary aligns with the duration of 
the legal contract of the underlying insurance contracts.  
Insurance acquisition cash flows 
Identification and treatment 
Insurance acquisition cashflows arise from the Company’s activities of selling, underwriting, and starting a group 
of insurance contracts that are directly attributable to the portfolio of insurance contracts to which the group 
belongs. 
The Company allocates insurance acquisition cashflows that are directly attributable to a group of insurance 
contracts to that group and to future groups that include renewals of those contracts, using a systematic and 
rational method. The allocation to future groups that include renewals only applies to YRT contracts and is 
broadly based on the way the Company expects to recover those insurance acquisition cashflows. For other 
contracts (primarily level premium contracts), insurance acquisition cashflows are included in the measurement of 
the current group. 
The resulting assets for insurance acquisition cashflows for YRT contracts are included in the carrying amount of 
the related portfolio of insurance contracts, tested for recoverability at each reporting date, and derecognised 
when each of the related future groups of insurance contracts are recognised. 
Recoverability assessment 
At each reporting date, the Company: 
—
recognises an impairment loss in the statement of comprehensive income if that is required so that the 
carrying amount of each asset for insurance acquisition cash flows does not exceed the expected net 
cash inflow for the related group; and 
—
recognises an impairment loss in the statement of comprehensive income to the extent that the parts of 
the assets for insurance acquisition cash flows resulting from insurance acquisition cash flows to each 
current or past group of insurance contracts exceeds the expected net cash inflow for the expected 
renewals relating to each such group and to the extent that this excess has not already been recognised 
as an impairment loss above. 
Net cash inflows for each group, for purposes of recoverability assessment, is determined on the basis of 
applying discounted present value of future cashflows for the expected term of the group of contracts and 
renewals applicable to that group of contracts. This expected term may differ to the duration utilised for the 
systematic attribution of insurance acquisition cashflows. 
Medical policies are projected to renew across a longer time duration than other insurance contracts due to the 
nature of the insurance cover provided and because of this extended renewal nature the lifetime expected 
premium profile differs materially to that of other contracts. This has been included as a factor in the projection of 
future cashflows arising from those renewals, allowing for lapse assumptions, solely for the purposes of 
determining recoverability of the asset for insurance acquisition cash flows associated with medical insurance 
contracts.
Additionally, net cash inflows, for purposes of recoverability assessment of all assets for insurance acquisition 
cash flows, may include assumptions relating to credible future premium and operating expense changes which 
differ to those used for measurement outlined below.  
The Company reverses any impairment losses in profit or loss and increases the carrying amount of the related 
asset(s) to the extent that the impairment conditions have improved.

Measurement – General model 
The Company applies the General Measurement Model (‘GMM’), the default measurement model under NZ IFRS 
17, for all its insurance contracts issued and reinsurance contracts held. 
Insurance contracts – initial recognition
At initial recognition, insurance contracts are measured by the Company as the total of (a) the fulfilment 
cashflows, which comprise estimates of the present value of future cashflows that are expected to arise as the 
Company fulfils the contracts during the NZ IFRS 17 contract boundary and an explicit risk adjustment for non-
financial risk, and (b) the Contractual Service Margin (‘CSM’).   
The Company’s objective in estimating future cashflows is to determine an amount equal to the expected value, 
or the probability-weighted mean, of the full range of possible outcomes, considering all reasonable and 
supportable information available at the reporting date without undue cost or effort and considering a range of 
scenarios which have commercial substance and give a good representation of possible outcomes.  
Estimated future cashflows have been discounted using risk free yield curves adjusted to reflect the liquidity 
characteristics of the contracts by using the spread of corporate bonds over swaps or bonds issued by the 
Australian government. 
The yield curves were based on the liquid risk-free yield curve and adjusted for the cash flow and liquidity 
characteristics of the group of insurance contracts. The liquidity characteristics reflected the comparable 
instrument for which market information was available.   
The risk adjustment for non-financial risk is determined by the Company as the compensation that the Company 
requires for bearing the uncertainty about the amount and timing of the cash flows that arise from non-financial 
risk. 
Risk adjustments for non-financial risk are estimated using a cost of capital technique. The cost of capital 
approach is based on the concept of holding sufficient capital as a buffer against a wide spectrum of risks, and 
there is a financial or opportunity cost to hold the present value of all these required amounts over the lifetime of 
the insurance contracts. 
This corresponds with a target confidence level at the 75th percentile on the excess value at risk on the expected 
present value of future cashflows. 
The CSM represents the unearned profit of a group of insurance contracts that the Company expects to 
recognise as it provides services. At initial recognition, the group of insurance contracts is not onerous if the total 
of the following is a net inflow: 
—
the fulfilment cash flows; 
—
any cash flows arising at that date; and 
—
any amount arising from the derecognition of any assets or liabilities previously recognised for cash 
flows related to the group including derecognition of assets for insurance acquisition cash flows. 
For non-onerous groups of insurance contracts, the CSM is measured as the equal and opposite amount of the 
net inflow, which therefore results in no income or expenses arising on initial recognition. If the total is a net 
outflow, then the group of insurance contracts is onerous. The net outflow is then recognised as a loss in the 
statement of comprehensive income. Subsequent improvement in fulfilment cashflows results in a reduction of 
the loss component for onerous contracts. Such reductions are immediately recognised in the statement of 
comprehensive income. 
For groups of contracts acquired in a transfer of contracts or a business combination, the Company includes the 
consideration paid for the contracts in the fulfilment cash flows as a proxy for the premiums received at the date 
of acquisition. In a business combination, the consideration received is determined as the fair value of the 
contracts at that date. 
Insurance contracts – subsequent measurement 
The carrying amount of a group of insurance contracts on subsequent measurement at each reporting date is the 
sum of the liability for remaining coverage and the liability for incurred claims. The liability for remaining coverage 
comprises (a) the fulfilment cashflows that relate to services that will be provided under the contracts in future 
periods and (b) any remaining CSM at that date. The liability for incurred claims comprises the fulfilment 
cashflows for incurred claims and expenses that have not yet been paid, including claims that have been incurred 
but not yet reported.

The Company adjusts the CSM in subsequent reporting periods for interest accretion and only for those changes

 Reinsurance contracts – initial recognition 
The Company applies the same accounting policies to measure groups of reinsurance contracts, with the 
following modifications:  
—
the carrying amount of a group of reinsurance contracts at each reporting date is the sum of the asset 
for remaining coverage and the asset for incurred claims. The asset for remaining coverage comprises 
(a) the fulfilment cashflows that relate to services that will be received under the reinsurance contracts in 
future periods and (b) any remaining CSM at that date. 
—
the Company measures the estimates of the present value of future cashflows using assumptions that 
are consistent with those used for the underlying insurance contracts with an adjustment for any risk of 
non-performance by the reinsurer. The effect of the non-performance risk of the reinsurer is assessed at 
each reporting date and the effect of changes in the risk is recognised in the insurance service result in 
the statement of comprehensive income. 
—
the Company determines the risk adjustment for non-financial risk based on the amount of risk being 
transferred to the reinsurer. 
The CSM of a group of reinsurance contracts represents the net cost or gain on purchasing reinsurance. It is 
measured such that no income or expense arises on initial recognition. 
Reinsurance contracts – subsequent measurement 
The Company adjusts the CSM in subsequent reporting periods for interest accretion and only for those changes 
in the fulfilment cashflows that relate to future services. The CSM is then recognised in the statement of 
comprehensive income as reinsurance services are received. 
An exception to the above is that the Company recognises income when it recognises a loss on onerous 
underlying contracts if the reinsurance contract is entered into before or at the same time as the onerous 
underlying contracts are recognised. In this case, a loss-recovery component is created which determines the 
amounts that are subsequently excluded from the determination of the allocation of reinsurance premiums paid, 
amounts recoverable from reinsurers, and reinsurance finance income. Reversals and other changes in related 
loss components of onerous contracts result in corresponding reversals and changes in the loss-recovery 
components of reinsurance contracts. Such reversals and changes in loss-recovery components are immediately 
recognised in the statement of comprehensive income. 
Derecognition and contract modification
The Company derecognises insurance contracts and reinsurance contracts when: 
—
the rights and obligations relating to the contract are extinguished (i.e., discharged, cancelled, or 
expired); or 
—
the contract is modified such that the modification results in a substantially different contract boundary or 
the modified contract would have been included in a different group of contracts. The Company then 
derecognises the initial contract and recognises the modified contract as a new contract. 
If a contract is derecognised because its terms are modified, the CSM of the group from which the contract is 
derecognised is adjusted for the resultant change in fulfilment cashflows.

10. Insurance and reinsurance contracts (continued)
Presentation
The Company presents separately in the statement of financial position the portfolios of insurance contracts that 
are assets and those that are liabilities, and portfolios of reinsurance contracts that are assets and those that are 
liabilities.  
Assets for insurance acquisition cash flows are included in the carrying amount of the related portfolios of 
insurance contracts issued. 
The Company disaggregates the amounts recognised in the statement of comprehensive income into an 
insurance service result, comprising insurance revenue and insurance service expenses, and insurance finance 
income or expenses. 
The Company disaggregates the changes in risk adjustment for non-financial risk between the insurance service 
result and the insurance finance income or expenses. 
Income and expenses from reinsurance contracts are presented separately from income and expenses from 
insurance contracts. Income and expenses from reinsurance contracts, other than insurance finance income or 
expenses, are presented on a net basis as ‘net expenses from reinsurance contracts’ in the insurance service 
result. 
Insurance revenue and insurance service expenses exclude any investment components. 
Insurance revenue 
The Company’s insurance revenue represents the provision of services arising from a group of insurance 
contracts at an amount that reflects the consideration to which the Company expects to be entitled in exchange 
for those services. It represents the total of the changes in the liability for remaining coverage that relate to 
services for which the Company expects to receive consideration, and comprises the following items: 
—
claims and other insurance service expenses incurred in the year, measured at the amounts expected at 
the beginning of the year. 
—
the expected change in the risk adjustment for non-financial risk relating to current services. 
—
the release of the CSM based on the coverage units provided during the period and expected to be 
provided in future periods within the coverage period.  
—
an allocation of premiums that relate to recovering insurance acquisition cashflows. 
Where relevant, the above items exclude amounts related to the loss component, if any, and amounts included in 
insurance finance expense. 
For determining the release of the CSM, coverage units are determined as the quantity of services provided in 
the period and expected to be provided in future periods within the coverage period. Coverage units are 
calculated as the maximum contractual cover (quantity of benefits provided) as projected across the coverage 
period, allowing for claims and lapses.
The allocation of premiums that relate to recovering insurance acquisition cash flows to each period is 
determined in a systematic way based on the passage of time. An equal amount is included in insurance service 
expenses. 
Loss components 
The Company establishes a loss component of the liability for remaining coverage for onerous groups of 
insurance contracts. The loss component is updated based on a systematic allocation of the subsequent changes 
relating to current services in the outgo related components of the fulfilment cash flows. The Company has 
applied the proportion that the loss component represents of the estimated future outgo and risk adjustment at 
initial recognition or at the start of the Company’s financial year to determine the systematic allocation.

10. Insurance and reinsurance contracts (continued)
Insurance service expenses 
Insurance service expenses comprise incurred claims cost, change in claims cost related to past service, 
amortisation of insurance acquisition cash flows and other incurred insurance service expenses (e.g., losses on 
onerous contracts & reversals of such losses, impairment losses on assets for insurance acquisition cash flows & 
reversals of such impairment losses) directly related to fulfilment of insurance contracts. 
Impairment losses on assets for insurance acquisition cash flows are determined through a forward looking 
analysis of expected future cash flows discounted using projected future rates. This analysis allows for assumed 
renewal patterns relating the underlying insurance contracts, projected maintenance expenses, and claims 
assumptions, for the expected life of the insurance contracts forming the groups and portfolios. Allowance is 
made for premium increases to the extent they are expected to arise from standard contractual adjustments.
Expenses that relate directly to the fulfilment of contracts are recognised in the statement of comprehensive 
income as insurance service expenses, when they are incurred in the case of maintenance expenses and subject 
to allocation over time in the case of acquisition expenses. Expenses that do not relate directly to the fulfilment of 
contracts are presented outside the insurance service result.  
Investment components are not included in insurance revenue and insurance service expenses under NZ IFRS 
17 and are defined as the amount, if any, that the Company would be required to repay to the policyholder in all 
circumstances, regardless of whether an insured event occurs. The Company has assessed that it does not have 
any investment components in the insurance contracts it currently issues but some of the reinsurance contracts it 
currently holds include investment components as so defined. 
Net income or expenses from reinsurance contracts held 
Amounts recovered from reinsurers and reinsurance expenses are not presented separately in the statement of 
comprehensive income, instead being presented as net expenses from reinsurance contracts in the insurance 
service result. Additional information about the reinsurance contracts held are included in the disclosures of the 
reconciliation of the movements of the reinsurance contract assets and liabilities. 
 Insurance finance income and expenses 
Changes in the carrying amounts of groups of insurance contracts arising from the effects of the time value of 
money, financial risk, and changes therein are presented by the Company as insurance finance income or 
expenses.
The Company made an accounting policy choice to present insurance finance income or expenses in the 
statement of comprehensive income. This accounting policy choice broadly aligns with the measurement 
approach of underlying investments.

Asset for insurance acquisition cash flows (‘AIACF’) impairment loss reversal 
As at 31 March 2024, $66.5 million of accumulated impairment losses had been recognised in the statement of

estimates of future claims, premiums, and operating expenses. Where such estimates are changed as a result of 
new developments or new information the impact of those changes is recognised prospectively in the period of 
the change and in future periods.
As a result of management actions during the current year, as well as assessing estimates of future pricing 
changes, and wider economic impacts, $39.1 million of the previously recognised impairment losses have been 
reversed in the statement of comprehensive income for the year ended 31 March 2025, and the carrying amount

Investments in government bonds  
The Company invests in government bonds with maturities ranging from 1 to 349 months to materially match the 
solvency liability and associated interest rate exposures resulting from movements in claim reserves.  
Investments in government bonds are measured at fair value at inception and at each reporting date, with 
changes recognised immediately in profit or loss.  
Measurement of fair values 
Fair values are categorised into different levels in a fair value hierarchy based on the inputs used in the 
evaluation techniques as follows: 
Level 1: quoted prices (adjusted) in active markets for identical assets or liabilities. 
Level 2: inputs other than quoted prices included in Level 1 that are observable for the asset or liability, either 
directly (i.e., as prices) or indirectly (i.e., derived from prices). 
Level 3: inputs for the asset or liability that are not based on observable market data (unobservable inputs). 
The fair value of investments in government bonds reflects the price that would be received to sell the 
government bonds. The fair value measurement for the investments in government bonds has been categorised 
as Level 1 fair value based on quoted prices for identical assets in the active market. The fair value at balance 
date was derived from observable market prices quoted for each government bond at 31 March 2025. The total 
revaluation loss on investments in government bonds for the year ended 31 March 2025 is $0.5 million (31 March 
2024: $0.8 million loss).
Credit risk 
The Company is exposed to credit risk arising from investments in government bonds. At 31 March 2025, the 
maximum exposure to credit risk of the investments in government bonds designated as measured at fair value 
through profit or loss is their carrying amount of $29.8 million (31 March 2024: $21.7 million). The change in fair 
value attributable to changes in credit risk is determined based on the changes in the prices of credit-default 
swaps referenced to similar obligations of New Zealand Government, as these swaps best reflect the market 
assessment of credit risk for the government bonds. The increase in fair value of investments in government 
bonds attributed to credit risk, for the year ended 31 March 2025 is nil (31 March 2024: nil).

Scenario analysis 
Scenario analysis is the process of constructing and evaluating plausible and challenging scenarios, in order to 
test the preparedness to unfavourable future states. It is especially useful for considering a long-term horizon, for 
risks which are deeply uncertain, such as climate risk.
The Company conducted scenario analysis for the first time in the FY23 year, and built upon this experience for 
this financial year’s analysis:
—
A core team was established with members of the Climate Disclosure Working Group (see the 
Governance section).
—
The focal question formulated was the same as last year: “How could climate change affect our 
business model, impact our mid-term strategy, and what actions may be necessary to address these 
impacts?”
—
The scenarios written last year were deemed to be still relevant and were re-used, with their 
characteristics described in more detail below. It is to be noted however that the plausibility of a 1.5°C 
temperature outcome in 2050 diminishes in the light of 2024 being the warmest year on record, with 
2023 a close follower2,3,4.
—
The scenario analysis workshops gathered subject matter experts from strategy, product, finance, 
actuarial, operations, and risk functions. The workshops aimed to identify the climate-related risks and 
opportunities most relevant to the Company’s strategy, and to explore the magnitude of their impact 
across different time horizons and the three scenarios selected. No modelling was undertaken for the 
purpose of scenario analysis during FY24.
The Company conducts its scenario analysis on a standalone basis. The scenario analysis documentation, 
summing up the process and the outcome of the analysis, was presented to our Climate Disclosure steering 
committee and Risk Committee. Upon review, these committees have the opportunity to provide comments and 
revisions, which are then incorporated into the document. The Climate Disclosure steering committee endorsed 
the finding of no material climate-related risks and opportunities facing the Company in the short to medium term.

Targets
The Company is part of the DIL Group. The DIL Group has established a range of decarbonisation targets, 
across the different emissions groups: direct emissions (for Scope 1 and 2), operational emissions (all of Scope 3 
except category 15 – investments), and investment emissions.21
The Company has adopted a similar approach, aligned with DIL’s approach, including the following targets:
—
For direct emissions (Scope 1 and 2), from a baseline of FY24, a reduction of 33% by financial year 
2030 i.e. 0.0374 tCO2e / m$, and reaching net zero by financial year 2040.
—
For operational emissions (Scope 3, excluding emissions for investments), the Company will use a 
baseline of FY25. The target currently intended is a reduction of 20% by financial year 2030, and 
reaching net zero by financial year 2050.
These targets are intensity targets (i.e. tCO2e / m$ of insurance revenue), because the Company is still in a 
growth phase. However, the absolute emissions will also be tracked by management, as an intensity target may 
be insufficient to ensure actual emissions are driven down on its own.
—
For investments emissions, the Company aims to reach net zero by financial year 2050. However, there 
is no current interim target as the investment portfolio and SIPO are under review. 
DIL Group has published emissions-reduction targets which it considers are aligned with limiting global warming 
to 1.5℃ and for which it intends to obtain external certification.22 The Company takes comfort that its own targets 
are based on the same underlying assumptions and pathways as DIL Group. 
The targets described above do not rely on offsets although it is possible that offsets may be used to contribute to 
projects aligned to the Company’s environmental strategy.
